s: a king and his knights turned to stone
w: High on the limestone ridge, the Rollright Stones stand in open pasture among grazing sheep. There are three elements: the near-complete King's Men circle, the collapsed Whispering Knights dolmen nearby, and the lone King Stone across the road. The prehistoric facts are impressive — the Whispering Knights date to the early Neolithic, the circle to the late Neolithic or early Bronze Age. But it is the later folklore that gives the place its charge. A king and his army were marching across the hills when a witch challenged him: take seven strides and, if he could see Long Compton, he would become king of England. On the seventh stride a mound rose to block his view. She turned them all to stone. Local tradition adds further rules: it is impossible to count the King's Men three times and reach the same number. On New Year's Eve the stones are said to walk to a nearby stream to drink. Stand inside the circle on a quiet afternoon. The wind moves through the stones. The modern world feels far away. Whether you believe the witch's story or not, the place holds an ancient, slightly uneasy intelligence.
